name: Selling Online in Africa (WhatsApp Business, Marketplaces and Social Media)
objectives: Given your products, your customers and two or three online channels, choose where to sell online and write down why, naming the cost, the effort and who buys there for each channel
Using a phone with the WhatsApp Business app, set up a business profile and a product list with prices, with name, short description, hours, area served and at least three products
Given one of your products, take a clear photo and write a listing with a title, price, details and delivery, so a customer could order without asking a basic question

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Choosing where to sell online
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose one or two places to sell online that fit your products and customers.
This lesson builds toward: Given your products, your customers and two or three online channels, you will choose where to sell online and write down why, naming the cost, the effort and who buys there for each channel.
You do not need to be everywhere. Choose where your customers already are, and where you can keep up with messages. Selling online is like opening a second stall: it only works if someone is there to serve.
Chat apps such as WhatsApp are good for regular customers and neighbours. Social media such as Facebook, Instagram and TikTok helps new people discover you with photos and short videos. Marketplaces such as Jumia, Jiji, Kilimall and Konga already have many buyers searching, but they have rules, and some take a commission (a part of each sale) or charge for promoted adverts.
For each channel, write three things: who buys there, what it costs (data, commission, adverts, delivery) and how much time it takes each day. Example: Ama in Kumasi sells beads. She keeps WhatsApp for her regular customers and adds Instagram to reach new buyers in Accra. A shoemaker in Dakar might start with WhatsApp and Facebook, then add a marketplace later.
Before you join a marketplace, read its seller page: what it charges, how it pays you, when, and what happens with returns. These change, so check the marketplace's own website, not a forwarded message.
Step by step:
- List where your customers already chat, scroll and shop.
- For each channel, write who buys there, the cost and the time it takes.
- Choose one main channel and, at most, one more.
- For a marketplace, read its own seller page for fees, payment and returns.
Words to know:
- Channel: a place where you sell or talk to customers, such as WhatsApp, Facebook or a marketplace.
- Marketplace: a website or app where many sellers list products and buyers search, such as Jumia or Jiji.
- Commission: a part of each sale that a marketplace keeps as its fee.
Try it now: Draw a small table with your two or three possible channels. For each, write who buys there, what it costs and the time it takes. Circle the one you will start with.
You can now compare online channels by cost, effort and customers, and choose where to start.

check.q: You can answer messages for one hour a day. What is the best start?
options: Open accounts on six apps at once
Start with one main channel you can keep up with
Pay for adverts before you have a product list
check.why: A channel only works if you answer customers, so start with what you can keep up with.

check.q: Where do you check what a marketplace charges sellers?
check.why: Fees and rules change, and only the marketplace's own page is reliable.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Setting up WhatsApp Business: profile and product list
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Set up a WhatsApp Business profile and a product list with prices.
This lesson builds toward: Using a phone with the WhatsApp Business app, you will set up a business profile and a product list with prices, with name, short description, hours, area served and at least three products.
WhatsApp Business is a separate app from normal WhatsApp, made by the same company for small businesses. Get it only from the official app store (Google Play on Android). It lets you show a business profile, show your products with prices, and send greeting and away messages.
Your business profile is your shop sign. Fill in your business name, a short description of what you sell, your area or address, your opening hours, and how customers can pay. Use a clear logo or a photo of your stall or best product.
Then add your products to the product list (the app calls it a catalogue in many versions): a photo, a name, a price in your currency and a short description. Customers can look through it and send you an item in the chat. Example: Wanjiku in Nakuru adds "Maasai beaded sandals, size 37-41, KES 1,200" (an example price).
Menus differ between phones and versions. If you cannot find a setting, open the app's settings and look for business tools. You can also set a short greeting message for new customers and an away message for when you are closed.
Step by step:
- Install WhatsApp Business from the official app store.
- Fill in the business profile: name, description, area, hours, payment methods.
- Add a logo or a clear photo.
- Add at least three products with photo, name, price and short description.
- Set a greeting message and an away message.
Words to know:
- Business profile: the page that shows your business name, description, hours and location to customers.
- Product list (catalogue): a list of your products with photos and prices that customers can look through in the app.
- Away message: an automatic reply sent when you are closed.
Official sources:
- WhatsApp Business: the WhatsApp Business app (business profile, showing products and prices, greeting and away messages)
Try it now: Install WhatsApp Business (or open it if you have it). Fill in your profile and add three products with a photo, a name, a price and one line of description. Ask a friend to look at it and tell you one thing that is unclear.
You can now set up a WhatsApp Business profile and a product list that customers can browse.

check.q: Which detail belongs in your business profile?
check.why: Hours tell customers when you will answer; PINs, passwords and customer numbers stay private.

check.q: A product in your list shows a photo but no price. What do you add?
options: A long story about the shop
check.why: A clear price saves time and stops customers leaving without asking.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Photos and listings that sell
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Take a clear product photo and write a listing a customer can order from.
This lesson builds toward: Given one of your products, you will take a clear photo and write a listing with a title, price, details and delivery, so a customer could order without asking a basic question.
A customer online cannot touch your product, so the photo and words must do the job. Take photos in daylight near a window or outside in the shade. Use a plain background such as a cloth or a wall. Wipe the camera lens. Show the whole product, then one close-up, and something that shows size, such as a hand.
A good listing answers the customer's questions before they ask: a clear title (what it is), the price in your currency, size, colour, quantity or weight, what it is made of, and how and where you deliver. Example: "Shea butter body cream, 250 g jar, unscented, GHS 60. Delivery in Tamale today; other towns by bus parcel." (an example price).
Be honest. Show the real product, not a picture from the internet, and say if colours vary. Honest photos mean fewer returns and more trust. Keep files small to save data: one clear photo is better than ten blurry ones.
Step by step:
- Clean the product and the camera lens.
- Use daylight and a plain background.
- Take one full photo, one close-up and one that shows size.
- Write title, price, size or weight, material, and delivery.
- Read it as a customer: can you order without asking a question?
Words to know:
- Listing: the photo and words that show one product for sale.
- Close-up: a photo taken near the product to show detail.
Try it now: Choose one product. Take three photos (whole, close-up, size) in daylight on a plain background. Write a listing with title, price, details and delivery. Read it as a customer and fix anything you would have to ask about.
You can now take clear product photos with a basic phone and write a listing that customers can order from.

check.q: Where is the best light for a product photo?
options: Daylight near a window or in the shade
A dark room with the flash on
check.why: Soft daylight shows true colours and detail without hard shadows.

check.q: Which listing lets a customer order without asking?
options: "Brown leather handbag, 30 x 25 cm, NGN 18,000, delivery in Lagos in 2 days"
check.why: It gives what it is, size, price and delivery, so the customer can decide.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Selling, getting paid and delivering

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Answering customers and closing the sale
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Reply to a customer and confirm an order in one clear message.
This lesson builds toward: When a customer sends a question or an order, you will reply politely and confirm the order in writing, within your stated hours, with item, quantity, price, delivery and payment in one message.
Online, the seller who answers first and clearly often gets the sale. Reply within your opening hours, greet the customer, and answer the exact question. If you do not know, say when you will find out.
Save short replies you send often, such as your price list, delivery areas and payment options. WhatsApp Business lets you save replies and use them again; menus differ, so look in the business tools. This saves typing and keeps your answers the same every time.
When the customer is ready, confirm the order in one message: item, quantity, price, delivery place and cost, delivery day, and how they will pay. Ask them to reply "Yes" to confirm. Example from Abidjan: "Bonjour Awa. Order: 2 wax-print dresses, size M, 15,000 XOF each = 30,000 XOF. Delivery to Cocody on Saturday, 1,000 XOF. Payment by mobile money before delivery. Reply OUI to confirm." (example prices).
Stay polite, even when a customer bargains hard or is rude. Never send insults or post a customer's messages publicly.
Step by step:
- Greet the customer and answer the exact question.
- Use a saved reply for price lists, delivery and payment.
- Confirm: item, quantity, price, delivery place, cost and day, payment method.
- Ask the customer to reply "Yes" before you prepare the order.
Words to know:
- Saved reply (quick reply): a message you save in the app and send again with a few taps.
- Order confirmation: one message that lists everything the customer agreed to buy and how it will be paid and delivered.
Try it now: Write and save an order-confirmation message for your business with spaces for item, quantity, price, delivery and payment. Then fill it in for one pretend order.
You can now answer customers clearly and confirm every order in one written message.

options: "2 bags, KES 1,500 each = KES 3,000. Delivery to Kisumu town Friday, KES 200. Pay by M-Pesa. Reply YES."
check.why: It lists item, quantity, price, delivery and payment, and asks the customer to confirm.

check.q: Why save replies you send often?
options: So answers are fast and the same every time
So you can share customers' numbers
check.why: Saved replies save typing and keep your prices and rules consistent.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Getting paid safely: stop fake payment alerts
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Check that a payment has really arrived before you hand over goods.
This lesson builds toward: Before you send goods paid by mobile money or bank transfer, you will check in your own app or official provider message that the money has arrived, never trusting a screenshot, a forwarded message or a caller, and never sharing a PIN.
Many online sellers are paid by mobile money (M-Pesa, MTN MoMo, Orange Money, Wave) or bank transfer, or cash on delivery. Scammers know this. A common trick is a fake payment alert: a text, a screenshot or a forwarded message that looks like a payment but no money came.
Your rule: goods leave only when the money shows in your own account. Open your own mobile money or banking app, or dial your provider's official code, and check the balance or the transaction. A screenshot from the customer is not proof. A text from an ordinary phone number is not proof.
Another trick: "I sent you money by mistake, please send it back." Do not send anything. Check your balance yourself; if there is a real mistaken payment, your provider can reverse it through its own process. A real provider never asks for your PIN, your password or a one-time code. Never share them, not even with someone who says they are from the company.
For cash on delivery, count the cash before handing over the parcel, and know the notes of your currency. Each central bank publishes fraud warnings, for example the Central Bank of Kenya and the Central Bank of Nigeria.
Step by step:
- Agree the payment method in the order confirmation.
- When the customer says they paid, open your own app or dial your provider's official code.
- Check the amount and the sender in your balance or statement.
- Only then hand over or send the goods.
- Ignore "send back my mistaken money" requests; let the provider handle reversals.
Words to know:
- Fake payment alert: a text, screenshot or message made to look like a payment when no money was sent.
- PIN: your secret number for mobile money or your bank. Only you should know it.
- Reversal: when a payment is sent back; a real one is done by your provider, not by you sending money to a stranger.
Official sources:
- Central Bank of Kenya: fraud safety
- Central Bank of Nigeria: consumer protection
Try it now: Write your payment rule on paper and stick it near where you pack orders. Then practise: open your own mobile money or bank app and find where you see your last transaction.
You can now check that money has truly arrived in your own account before sending goods, and refuse fake payment and reversal tricks.

check.q: A customer sends a screenshot of a payment. What do you do?
options: Check your own app or official code for the money
Send them your PIN to check
check.why: Only your own account shows whether the money really arrived; screenshots can be faked.

check.q: Someone says they sent you money by mistake and asks you to send it back. What is safest?
options: Check your own balance and let your provider handle any reversal
Give them your PIN so they can take it
check.why: This is a common trick; a real mistaken payment is reversed through the provider.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Delivery, returns and keeping customers' trust
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a delivery and returns policy and keep customers' details private.
This lesson builds toward: When you deliver an order, you will write and follow a delivery and returns policy that protects customers' trust and data, stating delivery areas, cost, time and returns, and keeping customers' numbers private.
Customers come back when delivery is reliable. Write down your delivery areas, the cost to each, how long it takes and how you send: by hand, a motorbike rider (boda boda or okada), a bus parcel service or a courier. Pack goods well and send the customer a message when the parcel leaves, with the rider's name or the parcel number.
A returns policy says what happens if something is wrong: for example, "Wrong size? Tell us within 2 days and we will exchange it if it is unused." Keep it short and fair, and follow it every time. In Morocco, a seller in Casablanca might say: exchange within 3 days, customer pays return delivery unless the item is faulty.
Customers' phone numbers, addresses and orders are private. Do not share them, post them or add people to groups or broadcast lists without asking. Many countries have data protection laws, for example Kenya's Data Protection Act and the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023. When you are not sure what applies, check your national data protection office.
After delivery, ask if all is well and invite a review or a photo you may share, with their permission.
Step by step:
- Write delivery areas, costs, times and how you send.
- Pack well and send a message when the parcel leaves.
- Write a short, fair returns policy and follow it.
- Keep customers' numbers and addresses private; ask before adding anyone to a list.
- Ask for feedback after delivery.
Words to know:
- Returns policy: your rule for what happens when a customer wants to return or exchange a product.
- Broadcast list: a list in WhatsApp for sending one message to many contacts; only people who saved your number receive it.
- Personal data: information about a person, such as their name, phone number or address.
Official sources:
- Office of the Data Protection Commissioner, Kenya (Data Protection Act, 2019)
- Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC): Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023
Try it now: Final task: put together your one-page online shop plan: where you sell and why, your profile text, three listings, your saved order confirmation, your payment rule, and your delivery and returns policy.
You can now deliver reliably, handle returns fairly and keep your customers' details private.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Where to sell No channel chosen, or many channels with no reason. One or two channels chosen, with who buys there, the cost and the time for each. Also says what would make you add or drop a channel after three months. Profile and product list Profile missing name, hours or area, or fewer than three products. Profile with name, description, area, hours and payment, plus at least three products with prices. A friend or customer browsed it and one unclear point was fixed. Listings Blurry or borrowed photos, or no price or delivery. Three listings with real, clear photos, title, price in local currency, details and delivery. Each listing has a close-up and a size photo, and honest notes such as colour variation. Order confirmation No saved confirmation, or details missing. A saved message with item, quantity, price, delivery place, cost and day, payment, and a request to reply Yes. Saved replies for prices, delivery and payment as well. Payment rule Goods may leave on a screenshot or promise, or the PIN is shared. Written rule: goods leave only when money shows in your own account; never share a PIN or code. Also covers mistaken-payment requests and counting cash on delivery. Delivery, returns and data No delivery details or returns rule, or customer data is shared. Delivery areas, cost, time and method, a short returns policy, and a promise to keep customer data private. Customers are asked before being added to any list, and feedback is asked after delivery. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What should a delivery policy include?
options: Delivery areas, cost, time and how you send
check.why: Areas, cost, time and method tell customers exactly what to expect.

check.q: You want to send a weekly price list to customers. What is right?
options: Post all their numbers in a public group
Sell their numbers to another trader
Add strangers from a bought list
Ask customers first and keep their numbers private
check.why: Customers' numbers are personal data; ask before you message them in bulk.
